name: University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good landing page
title: University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good landing page
answer: This is the University of Notre Dame's Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good landing page, directed by Meghan Sullivan. It describes a multidisciplinary community for moral understanding and AI technology ethics, with practical models for ethical design, development and deployment. Its most useful point for faith readers is Sullivan's warning that many AI industry workers talk flippantly about job displacement and cheaper, faster AI work, while some seek to transcend work for family and hobbies. It also names Lily Abadal and the DELTA project on human formation in the age of AI.

sections.body: The University of Notre Dame publishes this page for the Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, which is directed by Meghan Sullivan. It is an institutional landing page rather than a full report or study. It sets out the institute's aim to convene a multidisciplinary community, advance moral understanding and respond to pressing ethical issues. Its stated scope includes interdisciplinary research, thought and policy leadership in artificial intelligence and other technology ethics. The text does not state a publication or update date.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The page presents the Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good as a multidisciplinary community that advances moral understanding and develops responses to pressing ethical issues of the era. It says the institute promotes broad based, far reaching interdisciplinary research, thought and policy leadership in artificial intelligence and other technology ethics. It engages relevant stakeholders to examine real world challenges and to provide practical models and applied solutions for ethical technology design, development and deployment. The page also carries comments from Meghan Sullivan, described as a Catholic philosopher at the University of Notre Dame who often meets with AI leaders and developers. She said many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and about AI being able to do work faster and cheaper. Some, she said, are trying to transcend work and get to a place where they devote all their time to family and hobbies, like gardening and crafts. The page adds that AI awareness has been evolving, according to Lily Abadal. It identifies her as a partner at Catholic school consultants Partners in Mission, a professor at the University of South Florida and a faculty fellow with a project at the University of Notre Dame called DELTA, Human Formation in the Age of AI.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The text gives no numerical figures. It attributes to Meghan Sullivan the position that many AI industry workers talk very flippantly about job displacement and about AI doing work faster and cheaper, and that some seek to transcend work for family and hobbies. It attributes to Lily Abadal the view that AI awareness has been evolving, and it identifies her roles at Partners in Mission, the University of South Florida and the DELTA project, Human Formation in the Age of AI.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in churches and faith organisations would use this page to see how a Catholic university institute frames AI ethics as a matter of moral understanding and human formation. The page links AI ethics to practical design, development and deployment, and it names a project, DELTA, Human Formation in the Age of AI, that speaks directly to formation concerns. Sullivan's comments about work, displacement and the desire to transcend work give a faith informed voice on how AI changes labour and daily life. The page is useful as a signpost to Notre Dame activity and to Catholic school consulting rather than as a detailed industry report.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Churches and Faith Organisations

sections.body: This is a short institutional landing page, not a study, report or peer reviewed article. It does not give publication or update dates, research findings, data, methodology or detailed examples. It does not explain how churches or faith organisations should use AI, and it does not describe the DELTA project beyond its name and the phrase Human Formation in the Age of AI. The page is institutional and partial in scope, and it does not sell a product. Any reader needing evidence or practical guidance would have to go beyond this text.
